problem: Speaker-Follower style data augmentation for R2R samples shortest paths, which encode environment-specific biases over the agent's teleporting action space (action priors), so agents overfit to seen environments and generalize poorly to unseen ones despite more synthetic data.
motivation: R2R has few human-annotated instructions, so synthetic augmentation is standard, yet a large seen/unseen gap remains. The authors observe that a greedy agent using only edge-traversal statistics from shortest-path data, with no language, already gets over half of the Follower's seen-environment success, suggesting agents can exploit priors rather than language.
key_idea: Augment R2R with Speaker-annotated random-walk paths (non-shortest, avoiding revisits) whose action distribution is near uniform, removing scene-specific action priors and forcing reliance on language.
insight: Amount of augmented data is not the only factor; the path distribution matters. The MTM-greedy agent with no language reaches 0.35 SR vs 0.12 random (0.66 Follower) on val-seen, which shows the priors are exploitable. Random-walk augmentation gives lower seen performance but the best unseen SR (38.9 vs 33.8 for the next best), and the seen-to-unseen drop shrinks from 31.9 to 14.1 absolute points. Caveat: the random-walk model can only use teacher forcing, and the teacher-forced shortest baseline is the fairest comparison.
method: Action-prior analysis: build per-environment Markov transition matrices (MTM) from edge traversal counts in the Speaker-Follower augmented data and run a language-free greedy agent (T=5) on val-seen to quantify priors.
Skew factor: per node, the ratio of largest transition probability to the uniform probability; the random-walk data has 96% of nodes near 1, while shortest-path datasets are heavily skewed.

Random walk path sampler: sample a start viewpoint uniformly, sample a path length from the R2R train length distribution, random walk without revisiting nodes, and resample if the goal is under 3 m from the start.
Speaker (frozen): seq2seq with attention pretrained on R2R that annotates instructions for the sampled paths on the fly.

Follower: seq2seq navigation agent that mirrors the Speaker, trained by imitation with teacher forcing on random walks; 40k iterations on augmented data then 20k on R2R (batch size 64, Adam, lr 1e-4).

setting.backbone: Speaker-Follower seq2seq with attention (LSTM), trained from scratch (own re-implementation)
setting.training_data: R2R train (21,567 instruction sets) plus Speaker-generated instructions for random-walk paths sampled on the fly (same number of paths as Speaker-Follower augmented dataset)
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (36 discrete view vectors per viewpoint)

results: Random-walk augmentation reaches 38.9 SR / 36.0 SPL on R2R val-unseen, beating the best baseline in the same implementation (shortest augmentation + teacher forcing, 33.8 SR) and the original Speaker-Follower numbers (35.5 SR). On val-seen it is worse than shortest-path augmentation (53.0 vs 61.6 with student forcing), and the seen/unseen SR gap shrinks to 14.1 points from 31.9.
limitations: Random walks cannot use student forcing since shortest-path correction is unavailable, so only teacher forcing is trained, which confounds comparison with the best shortest-path baseline.
Small-scale evaluation: only val seen/unseen, no test-server results, and single runs with no variance reported; absolute SR is well below contemporaneous SOTA.
Seen-environment performance drops relative to shortest-path augmentation, and the causal link to action priors is only supported indirectly.
